Stool
STOOL
n. (a seat without a back; in Exodus, the birthing stool of the Hebrew midwives)
Old English stol, a seat or throne — the word once covered any seat, and narrowed later to a backless one. In 2 Kings it renders Hebrew kisse, a seat; in Exodus, obnayim, a pair of stones, the birthing stool.

Biblical Definition

The word carries two very different scenes. The first is quiet hospitality. The Shunammite woman perceives that Elisha is a holy man of God passing by continually, and says to her husband, Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick. Four items, named one by one: somewhere to sleep, somewhere to eat, somewhere to sit, and light. That is the whole architecture of hospitality, and it cost a woman who had no son a good deal of thought about a man who could not repay her. The second scene is the opposite of a welcome. Pharaoh instructs the Hebrew midwives: when ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools; if it be a son, then ye shall kill him. The stools here are the birthing stones, the place where a woman labours, turned by a king's decree into an execution site. But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive. Two stools: one set out for a prophet by a woman who feared God, one used against infants by a king who did not, and defied by two women who did.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a seat without a back; a little form consisting of a board with three or four legs, intended as a seat for one person.

STOOL, n. A seat without a back; a little form consisting of a board with three or four legs.

STOOL, n. The seat used in certain offices and conditions of life.

MIDWIFE, n. A woman that assists other women in childbirth.

CHAMBER, n. An apartment in an upper story, or in the story above the lower floor of a dwelling house.

HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 4:10 — "Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither."

Exodus 1:16 — "And he said, When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools; if it be a son, then ye shall kill him: but if it be a daughter, then she shall live."

Exodus 1:17 — "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive."

Hebrews 13:2 — "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

Modern Corruption

Hospitality has become entertaining — a performance for people who can reciprocate — and the midwives' defiance is claimed by every side of the abortion argument; Scripture names the stool in both scenes and says who feared God.

expand to see more

The Shunammite's four items rebuke the modern practice of hospitality almost by accident. She did not clean a house for guests who would return the favour; she built a room on the wall for a travelling preacher, furnished it plainly, and asked nothing. Christ states the principle: when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind; and thou shalt be blessed, for they cannot recompense thee. Where hospitality becomes entertaining, the guest list changes, the standard rises, and the poor stop being invited. A bed, a table, a stool and a candle are enough, and always were.

Exodus 1 is quoted constantly in the argument over the killing of infants, and it deserves to be, but the verse has more in it than a slogan. The midwives are named — Shiphrah and Puah, two working women whose names outlasted the Pharaoh's — and the text gives their reason: they feared God. They disobeyed the highest authority in the world, at risk of their lives, over the lives of children who were not theirs, and God dealt well with them and made them houses. That is the pattern for civil disobedience in Scripture: not conscience as preference, but the fear of God overriding a command to shed innocent blood, accepted with the consequences.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kisse (H3678), a seat or throne; obnayim (H70), the birthing stones; yare (H3372), to fear; meyalledet, the midwife.

expand to see more

Hebrew kisse (H3678) — a seat, and also a throne; the plain stool in Elisha's chamber shares a word with Solomon's throne.

Hebrew obnayim (H70) — a pair of stones; the birthing stool, and elsewhere the potter's wheel.

Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, to reverence; the stated reason the midwives disobeyed.

Hebrew ner (H5216) — a lamp; the fourth item the Shunammite set in the chamber.

Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers; the New Testament word rendered hospitality.

Usage

"“a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick” — the whole architecture of hospitality."

"“see them upon the stools” — a birthing place turned into a decree."

"“But the midwives feared God” — the reason given for the refusal."
